utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. I do understand that we have overcome the technical problems. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before we continue, I do understand that Mr. Krajisnik has worked yesterday on the text of P64A tab 698, and I just want to get it on my screen again. What Mr. Krajisnik did, as far as I understand, Mr. Krajisnik -- and before putting this to you, I first remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you've given -- what you tried to do is to see whether you could decipher the badly legible paragraph 10 of this document. May I invite the usher to put the -- I would say the work product of Mr. Krajisnik on the ELMO and I do understand that what we'll now see is the original bad legible text and also the typewritten transcript of this text, both in Cyrillic and in Latin script. Can the interpreters see it now? The first thing I'd like to verify, and perhaps we should do this after the break, after having given an opportunity to both parties to look at it and to see whether they would agree that this is the text as read by Mr. Krajisnik and whether this would be disputed, that this is the way how it should be read. Perhaps we make some copies and during the first break, that counsel, assisted by their -- assisted by those who can read and speak the language, verify whether this is a reasonable explanation of what is written there. I do not hear any objections. Mr. Registrar, you're invited to get that document back for the time being to make two copies of it, provide it to the parties and the Chamber would like to hear -- perhaps if you make a few extra copies so that the booth is provided, the different booths are provided with it as well so that we also could then check on whether the translation, as we found it in tab 698.1 is an accurate translation. Then, Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, we'll do that. Your Honour, it could be a reasonable explanation but wrong so we'll look to see whether it's actually what we can agree is the correct one but absolutely we will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the purpose of the exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We will do that as soon as we possibly can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, good morning. We were coming on to the 10th of May, Mr. Krajisnik, and a particular minute or record in question at the session of the national Security Council and government of Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is found in P64A, binder 22, tab 617.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the ERN there is 01245315.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the -- we know there was an assembly session coming up now on the 12th of May in Banja Luka. That's clearly on the record. We also know from your evidence that you had a fairly recently, doesn't matter exactly what day, returned from a trip away with Dr. Karadzic and Professor Koljevic in connection with the European Community negotiations. Now, first of all, immediately before the assembly session which was coming up on the 12th of May, what was the state of play as far as the European Community, Cutileiro talks were concerned?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Cutileiro talks had been frozen before the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And frozen for what reason and by what process?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the European Community in a way interrupted the negotiations for an indefinite period of time, probably because the last meeting had not - how shall I put this? - yielded any good results, and that is why we addressed that appeal at that session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was the suspension of those negotiations linked in any way with issues relating to cease-fires or alleged breaches of cease-fires?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot recall exactly what the reasons were, but the reasons were formulated by the European Community. Quite simply, in a way, they interrupted or suspended for a moment, not over the longer term, these negotiations and at that moment there was that kind of decision. Probably, well, actually I think that at that meeting where Mr. Izetbegovic did not want to come, saying that the cease-fire was being violated, and that he would not come as a sign of his protest, somebody else did come, as far as I can remember, but it was explained differently by our side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did you and Dr. Karadzic have the same reaction and the same view in relation to the suspension of the European Community talks?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Koljevic and I had the same view that negotiations should be continued as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there any dissent from that view among other senior figures in the -- among the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people who were in Pale and who took part in these consultative meetings all shared this view I think and there weren't any exceptions. However, there is always someone who voices a doubt as to whether negotiations can resolve anything. Because as they were saying then the Muslim side was sabotaging the negotiations. However, these were isolated views, people were saying that out of concern, so these were not really relevant views. Everybody wanted the negotiations to continue as soon as possible, or perhaps I should put it this way: A maximum majority wanted it that way. Perhaps somebody said something different but I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In what way was it that the Muslim side -- well, first of all, was it in your view correct that the Muslim side were sabotaging the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were confident, I have to say I was confident, if I'm talking about my own feelings, that this was done by the Muslim side because this was in their interest, not to have negotiations because they already had a recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina and through negotiations there would be a transformation of Bosnia-Herzegovina which was not in their interest. So there was this suspicion, I cannot say that it's 100 per cent correct but it's quite logical and that made us feel right in our belief that they did not want negotiations and that they were violating the cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What about the Croats? Were they at this point supporting or opposing or in any way sabotaging the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Croat side actively worked on rounding off their own ethnic areas but they were not opposed to continuing the talks. Quite simply, well, let me put it this way: The worst case scenario would be that they were neutral but they were more in favour of continuing the negotiations and bringing them to an end. It also suited them to have a third entity in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: During the talks, the EC talks, before they were suspended, had there been discussion of the actual war situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina outside Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean at the session, at the negotiations, at the conference itself, or are you referring to Pale?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, I'm referring to the negotiations with Mr. Cutileiro and the European Community representatives.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Because the other side kept giving this reason, well when I say the other side I mean the Muslim side, I beg your pardon, they thought that the negotiations should not continue because the cease-fire was being violated, that there is a war going on, that the war should be stopped and only then things could happen. So there were these mutual accusations. The European Community tried to act as an arbiter and tried to clarify certain matters or spell them out in an objective manner. Of course, it goes without saying that we accused them and they accused us. How should I put this? That's the way it was at this conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there a cease-fire agreed or imposed in relation to anywhere outside Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that you had occasion to see here the platform of Mr. Karadzic and that on the 12th of April, this cease-fire was signed, and that was valid for all of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That means that you agree to a cessation of hostilities but it mostly pertained to Sarajevo. How should I put this? That's where the fiercest conflict took place, and in the eyes of the European Community and the international community and all of us who were there and lived there. I'm sorry, the objections were for the most part that the cease-fire was being violated in Sarajevo. You're right. So those were the objections voiced at the conference, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, before the assembly session which we know was held in Banja Luka on the 12th of May, was there at any time in May, any attempt to hold an assembly session before the Banja Luka session?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my memory, there is -- how should I put it? This information exists, and I'm so sure of it but I couldn't double check it with other people. I scheduled a meeting in Pale, at Jahorina actually, and a small number of MPs came because the MPs from Krajina could not come actually from Banja Luka. And when we didn't succeed in that, then all of us, the MPs and all throws who were present there, got together and went to Banja Luka. I did not remember how it was that we went there but in the record, I saw, in Mr. Karadzic's remarks, that it was by plane that we went to Banja Luka. Now, scheduling a session, that is something I know. I know that we were sitting there and I know about that. But whenever I asked a MP or a deputy, I wanted to sort of double check, and to resolve this dilemma of mine, nobody seems to remember that. But then I remember this, the fact that a session was scheduled and that it failed, and that that is why we went to Banja Luka to have the session held there on the 12th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And at this time, in the period in the run-up to the Banja Luka assembly session, you were working every day, were you, Mr. Krajisnik, at the Kikinda building?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you were living there as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I forgot to say that. My family and I lived in Panorama actually, in a room, from the very outset. All the rest had rooms in Kikinda. Well, not everybody but a maximum majority. First I thought I was in Kikinda too but no, I wasn't. I was in Panorama from the very beginning all the way up to the arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And we heard some evidence already about the working arrangements in Kikinda. Mrs. Cenic gave evidence, you recall, Mr. Krajisnik. Was her description of the working arrangements with you in an office at the end of a corridor, Dr. Karadzic in a room on the other side of the corridor, was her description of the physical layout and arrangements in Kikinda accurate?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. We all had a small room each. Well, it wasn't an office space or anything. It wasn't like a suite. It was a small room, intended for the accommodation of people who were vacationing. He had one room, I had one room, Mr. Koljevic - what should I say -- everybody else? And we had a room which was a bit bigger, if I can put it that way, and that could have been, say, 12 square kilometres.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I mean the bigger room was 12 or 15 square meters, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's where we met and talked. That was it. It was upstairs. The secretary had another small room next to this room, and well, it wasn't that there were doors between the adjacent rooms. That is how we managed to get organised at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you had a secretary of the assembly, did you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The secretary of the assembly was Mr. Milos Savic, the late Milos Savic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And where did he work?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Likewise, he had a room where he slept and where he worked. I mean, I think he was there in Kikinda at first and I think that later he moved to Panorama as well, but he worked there in Kikinda all the time. I mean, until we left later. But while we were in Kikinda he worked there. I was talking about sleeping. Later he slept in Panorama but at that moment he slept and worked in Kikinda.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krajisnik, a question expressed generally, so do your best; if you need a more specific question say so, but at this time, in the run-up to the assembly meeting in Banja Luka, on the Bosnian Serb side, who was running the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At one moment, when the Presidency at the suggestion of -- well, I don't know whether it was anybody's suggestion, and it doesn't matter, but they certainly didn't do it on their own, they proclaimed the establishment of the Serb Territorial Defence. So it was the armed people, and everybody stood on their own ethnic lines. I mentioned yesterday that the Yugoslav People's Army was present. Up until this moment, that is to say up until the 12th of May, I think that all the way up to the attack against the column and the siege of the JNA barracks, I think that the JNA was neutral to a maximum. After that, they took care of themselves. How to get the resources out of the barracks, and soon they prepared to leave. That is to say, for the people who were not from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina to leave. I'm certain that at that time the Yugoslav People's Army did not take any active steps to the advantage of these Serb territorial forces unless barracks were attacked or unless they themselves were attacked. This was confirmed in this conversation between Mr. Smajic and General Gagic or rather Colonel Gagovic. There was a lot of proof. There is a hill above the Lukavica barracks that was the only barracks in the Serb territory. At this hill called Mojmilo, there were Muslim force that very often targeted the barracks and then possibly they would respond. I can say therefore that that goes for that area. As for Rajlovac, the JNA was there and the armed territorials were there, and the civilian population. I don't know who responded to what because when the barracks were attacked, everybody was attacked. That is my view of what was happening at the time. Now, in this Yugoslav People's Army, tank crews and artillery crews, as a rule, came from the area. As a rule, when the war broke out, everybody stayed in his own area. One should not preclude the possibility of these people using JNA equipment, and doing something in their own initiative, if I can put it that way, but the policy of the Yugoslav People's Army was to be equidistant to all the sides and to have the role of the intermediary. I absolutely know that on the basis of the conversation I had with Mr. Kukanjac, who was fully convinced that he could retain his role and play the role he was supposed to play. Whenever our people were being unrealistic. He said, "This is my mandate. That is not my mandate. I cannot do that," and so on and so forth. So the situation was roughly the way I presented it just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What did you understand, and I'm being as specific as I can on time, Mr. Krajisnik, if I talk about the immediate run-up to that session in Banja Luka. So we are talking about the 9th, 10th, 11th of May 1992. What did you personally understand the military situation to be in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still think what I thought then. When the conflict broke out, everyone stood on their ethnic border so to say. There were some shifts later on in Ilidzanska Opstina, and Rajlovac, and in Grbavica itself. Everyone stood on the borders of their settlements. The Serbs were on the periphery and the Muslims were in the town. Next to the centre of town, there was a large area called Hrasnica which was separated from the town by the airport. Where they took up positions on the 4th or 5th of April, those were more or less their ethnic areas. In my view, this was logical. Within a relatively large ethnic area, there may have been a enclave or two of other ethnicities in the Serb areas but for the most part the rest of the territory was inhabited by Serbs. As I explained, the territory of the town was far more Serb than Muslim, but in terms of population, it was the other way around, by far. Perhaps 80 to 20 per cent. In the areas around the town, there were perhaps 20 per cent and 80 per cent in the town centre. So this was the other way around. Territory did not properly represent the population numbers, because it was the areas around the town and the rural areas. I don't know whether I've answered your question. If I haven't, I'll be happy to say whatever is necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, what Serb forces did you understand at that time to be on the periphery, as -- to use your word, of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these were people from that settlement, from that area, local people, people who lived there. I really don't know whether there were any others from outside. I know for a fact that everybody was defending his own area. The people from Vraca were protecting their area, from the people from Zabrdje theirs, and so on. Of course, at points where the forces were contiguous, people would ask for assistance from the next village, and they would hold the line together, the demarcation line, that is, or rather the line of armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And in the hills surrounding Sarajevo, what forces did you understand to be there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was only one point in Sarajevo, and this was on the route I drew, near Grbavica, were the Serbs dominant. In other areas, it was the Muslims who predominated. From this point where the Serbs were, one could fire on Sarajevo. The Muslims were dominant on other points and they could fire on the outskirts, where the losses were less, the effects were less. That's why this image was created that it was the Serbs who were dominant around Sarajevo, because the population was dense there. When they were shooting at Lukavac, Rajlovac, and so on, the population was less dense so there were fewer casualties. They also used snipers and so on, but this was not so evident. In the meantime, I consulted some generals who understand these things and I can tell you precisely what the points were where they were dominant, in positions overlooking Sarajevo. You can see that on the map, the map I gave you with the demarcation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, concentrating for a moment on this forces, you said that at that one point near Grbavica, Serbs were dominant, and leaving aside the other areas for the moment, Mr. Krajisnik, what Serb forces did you understand to be there at that point near Grbavica where they were dominant?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a small correction. The Serbs were not dominant in Grbavica. They were in a hole there. It was at the top of Grbavica where there is a road; that's Vraca. There was a place there where there was a police school, and at one point on that road, the Serbs held a dominant point. So the connection between Grbavica and Lukavica, at that peak, that's where the Serbs were dominant. What were the force? I know that there were police forces and the territorial forces, the armed people. That's what I know was there. Later on, when Grbavica was taken, the JNA was stationed there. But in the taking or liberation of Grbavica, I don't think the JNA participated in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, at this point, still talking about these few days in the run-up to the Banja Luka assembly, was anybody in military command of such Serb forces as there were near Grbavica, as you've described?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There wasn't anyone from the military command. There was someone from the Territorial Defence. There is a telephone conversation of the 7th of May between a member of the MUP and a person from the Territorial Defence, and they were talking with me, because I, as a deputy and as a citizen of Sarajevo, wanted to know what was happening in Sarajevo. He told me that someone had carelessly come down from that hill in the direction of Grbavica and there were many military personnel residing in Grbavica and perhaps this was a Serb-majority area. He wanted to liberate this area but was not successful. Quite a lot of people were killed there. I wanted to know what had happened. And one of them said, "I'll come up there and tell you what this is all about."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krajisnik, in asking you whether anybody was in military command, I had intended military in a broad sense, not confined to army as opposed to Territorial Defence. So if you understand my question, please, in the broad sense of military command, was anybody in command of such Serb forces as there were near Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was an example of how these territorials acted on their own initiative. Somebody led that group down there and they suffered a defeat, and many men were killed. That's why I wanted to find out what had happened as a person from Sarajevo, and, of course, somebody organised -- or, rather, of course, had somebody organised this, I would have called him up and asked him, Why did you do this? But nobody knew who had taken these people down to Grbavica. You can see that from the telephone conversation. It was just an adventure that somebody embarked on and it ended up tragically. The JNA was over the hill in Lukavica. They did not participate in this. Those people thought they could do that easily, but to this very day, I can't recall who it was who did that. It wasn't the police. You can tell that from the telephone conversation. And who it was, I don't know. I mean, I don't know who organised it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, at this point in time, Mr. Krajisnik, you, the Bosnian Serb leadership in Pale, you did regard yourself, did you, as fighting a war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it was clear to us that the war had started. There was no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And were you, the Bosnian Serb leadership in Pale, were you trying to develop and implement a coordinated strategy for fighting that war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, I have to tell you about myself. When I sought information, I did so as a person who had lived in Sarajevo, and who was interested in what was happening and who was a deputy from the area. As a citizen, I wanted to know whether anyone had been killed or wounded and what the situation was. That was my approach to this problem. You saw that there was the Territorial Defence and Mr. Karadzic was supposed to coordinate the MUP, the National Defence and the Territorial Defence but he was not successful in coordinating them because at every point in every village, everybody stood on their own lines and they were only defending themselves. If there was an unwritten order or an implied order, it was to defend oneself, to avoid crimes and people being killed, and the politicians had to do their job in continuing the negotiations, stopping the war, and finding a solution. That's why, as a prerequisite for the continuation of negotiations, those cease-fires were signed, in order -- well, it's much easier to talk when there is no shooting than when there is fighting on the ground and you are negotiating and discussing a political solution. There was no strategy at that time. All the fighting was focused on our hopes that the JNA would play their role and defend us if we were attacked, and the Territorial Defence or rather the armed people, it wasn't a proper Territorial Defence, it was the armed people, everyone was defending their own lines. At that time I never heard anybody talk about any kind of active moves. I'm talking about the period up to the 12th of May when the army of Republika Srpska was established. Whether someone was doing this on the ground, on their own initiative, that's a different matter, but I never heard anything of that nature from Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Koljevic or Mrs. Plavsic and especially not from the commander of the defence or the Minister of Defence. I never heard that from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the commander of the defence, who was that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Minister of Defence was Mr. Subotic. That's who I was referring to. The commander of the Territorial Defence formally and briefly was a person called Lukic. I think his first name was Vidoje, but I can't be sure of his first name. Those were the people holding those posts. We didn't have anybody else. And it was the task of the coordinator to coordinate their work and that was Mr. Karadzic. But he was unable to establish any kind of coordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You mentioned Mr. Lukic before. Apart from the people you've just mentioned, was there anybody else who was regarded by you at that time as a senior military commander of the Bosnian Serb forces fighting a war against Muslims and also, of course, in various areas, Croats?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only armed force was still the police. That police had their minister, it was Mr. Stanisic. There was no other armed force. Everything we heard here about private armies and paramilitaries, if it did happen, it was all arranged by local people who were concerned because they did not have the forces to defend their territories. It was they who organised all this. I don't remember anyone recruiting any people from the circle you are mentioning at Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Up to the period when you held the assembly in Banja Luka, had Mr. Mladic come to Pale for any discussions about what was happening on the ground in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a brief period, I don't remember how long, before the assembly session, before Mr. Mladic became the commander of the Main Staff. He was standing in for Mr. Kukanjac and he became -- or rather he replaced Mr. Kukanjac and he became the commander of the 2nd military district and I know that he was at Lukavica. At one occasion I was at the airport or I was speaking to someone in Lukavica, I don't remember who, and then I spoke to him. His role in his conversations with us was not significant, although when he learned that he was going to be appointed commander, there was a certain amount of coordination. Just before going to Banja Luka with Mr. Ostojic, he visited Herzegovina and Kalinovik, and at that session he explains this. So there was some kind of link, but he wasn't reporting on what was happening on the ground. I don't remember ever sitting down with Mr. Mladic before the 12th of May for him to inform us about developments on the ground. He was focused only on getting men out of the barracks, which had still not been done. In parallel with the representatives of the JNA from Belgrade. And most of his activity was centred on that. And this was done quite separately from anything we were doing. He was doing this on his own, without any influence from the government or anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And during the period up to the Banja Luka assembly session, did any other senior military figures, using "military" again in the broad sense, Mr. Krajisnik, come to Pale to report what was happening on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that, but I can say that the representatives of the JNA were not duty bound to inform us, and they didn't do so, to the best of my recollection. They could volunteer information about the situation because they already recognised an additional opponent in the Muslim side. They had issued a communique saying that all barracks should be besieged and communications cut off for the JNA. But I don't remember somebody coming to a meeting to provide us with information because it was his duty or because he had to do it or wanted to. We took the initiative to find out what they were doing, but to small effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So if you'd been asked at that time, Mr. Krajisnik, who are your military commanders for the Bosnian Serbs, what would your answer have been?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have said we didn't have any military commanders and that every municipality was acting separately. I thought it was the commander of the Territorial Defence, then I thought it was the Minister of Defence, and then I saw that these people had no power and there was nothing in practice they could do. I would have said that the -- those who were protecting us and those in whom we placed our confidence was the JNA. I'm now speaking about what the situation was in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When did the planning of the establishment of a Bosnian Serb army begin?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were intimations and we knew that there was some kind of UN resolution and the Muslim side insisted on this, that the JNA had to withdraw from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I think that the resolution was passed at that time. And we were then in a quandary because we thought that the JNA would stay there for at least five years, as had been agreed in Skopje between Mr. Izetbegovic and the representative of the General Staff. We were in a quandary then because the JNA would withdraw and the JNA then meant all the active duty officers. We would be left only with armed, unorganised people, and I remember well on one occasion we contacted someone in Belgrade, I don't know what time it was exactly, to find out what the plan was. They had promised that the JNA would stay and now it was withdrawing. And I saw then Mr. Karadzic -- or rather, excuse me, the late Mr. Milosevic suggested that we set up our own army, and so then we discussed how this could be done. He was adamant that representatives of the JNA, who were not born in Bosnia and Herzegovina, could not remain, unless they declared themselves to be volunteers, and we were asked to suggest who the commander could be, who could set up his own staff and organise an army. I remember on one occasion, when we went to see Mr. Kukanjac, he spoke on the telephone to Mr. Mladic in Knin. He mentions this in an interview. Mr. Karadzic liked him as a commander and as a soldier. I mean, Mr. Mladic, because he was frequently in the newspapers, as he had been born in Bosnia-Herzegovina, his name was put forward, and all the soldiers and officers from Bosnia-Herzegovina who wanted to stay could stay on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. At first, let me just add there were different ethnicities, it wasn't only Serbs, but later on the men of other ethnicities left or went over to the Muslim army. That's how the process went. I don't think that we ever would have established our own army had the Yugoslav People's Army stayed behind. These armed people would have to be placed under the command of the Yugoslav People's Army. Now, why was this not the case at the time? Because the Yugoslav People's Army specifically in Sarajevo, Mladic, who was standing in for Mr. Kukanjac or rather who replaced Mr. Kukanjac, was only occupied with a single problem, and that is, how should I call this, those soldiers who were under siege in Sarajevo, to get them out, and then these talks, negotiations, whatever. You really couldn't talk to him about anything else then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, you said that when Mr. Milosevic suggested that you set up your own army, you said, and so then we discussed how this could be done. Who were the "we", anybody else for that matter, who were engaged in those discussions?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very often, Mr. Stewart, Your Honours, gentlemen of the Prosecution, I use the word "we" and now it seems as if I took part in something atom sometime. Well in this case, I did take part in it. So perhaps I should make this distinction. Now, why did I take part in this? Because the negotiating team, on one occasion took an opportunity, and I don't know what the occasion was, to discuss that question. Perhaps we were even invited because we were the ones who were representing the Serb people from Bosnia-Herzegovina in the negotiations any way, and then somebody invited us and we became, well -- well, we were invited to be informed about these problems. Of course, it had to do with the offices we held because before I was on the negotiating team, of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so that's why the three of us, perhaps it wasn't all three of us, perhaps it was somebody else too, I don't know that, but I know that Karadzic was there, I was there, and I'm convinced that the late Mr. Koljevic was there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, would you please say whether this was right, Mr. Krajisnik, what you appeared to be talking about in that last answer was discussions with people outside the Bosnian Serbs about the principle of having a separate army. Was that -- is that correct? That was what you were talking about then?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The principle then was that members of the Yugoslav People's Army, who had been born in Bosnia-Herzegovina, could stay in Bosnia-Herzegovina if they wished, and join our new army. I'm saying that when that was said, later on in the realisation, in that army there were Muslims and there were Croats who had been born in Bosnia-Herzegovina and they were there for a while then but then later they left the army of Republika Srpska, or rather the army of the Serb republic, and they joined the Muslim army, or they left the army altogether and went to Belgrade, where, of course, they were received and I don't know how their status was resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So, Mr. Krajisnik, among the Bosnian Serbs, who were involved in discussions and planning for the setting up of a new and separate Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was done by the Minister of Defence, along with a team that was around Mr. Mladic. I think that none of us took part in the law or the organisation. This was just brought to the assembly and we adopted it. Not only I, but my colleagues too, as far as I can remember. None of us took part in this. I remember some General Kovacevic, a lawyer who worked on this new law on defence, the army, and so on and so forth -- the organisation of the army, rather, on behalf of the General Staff. And he was indeed from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the team that -- you said you thought that was done by the Minister of Defence. That was Mr. Subotic, along with a team that was around Mr. Mladic. Are you able to say who were the members of that team around Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I wasn't very precise. I'm saying that if someone was in contact with this expert team, on behalf of the Serb republic, it was the Minister of Defence. I am convinced that even he did not significantly influence the establishment of these documents. It was this expert team established by Mr. Mladic that prepared all of that. I saw that this law itself was foreign to the Minister of Defence, and he made some objections in respect of this law even after it had been adopted. So that was the only link to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, let's consider directly some practical matters. Do you agree, if a new army is being set up, whatever its origin in some other army, it's got to -- there have got to be such things as laws and regulations, as you've indicated. There have got to be financial arrangements, there have got to be logistical arrangements, there have got to be uniforms at some point fairly early on. We can agree about all those practical things that would need to be done, can we, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right that that's the way it was supposed to be. At that meeting I remember very well, I put a question: Who is now going to pay these officers? We have no money. Then they made a promise and indeed they carried it out. Since these future officers were people who were members of the Yugoslav People's Army for many years, they would just pay these active-duty officers. They would pay those who would want to stay in Bosnia-Herzegovina of their own free will, and that was indeed carried through. All the rest, reserve officers, the army, everything else, all of that, the Territorial Defence too, all of that was - how should I put this? - all of that was supposed to be regulated later on we did regulate it. I don't know whether people were paid and how much they were paid, but they were paid a lot less than they were supposed to be paid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask one clarifying question? You said -- you are talking about the meeting. Is that a meeting -- which meeting exactly are you referring to? Is that a meeting with the late Mr. Milosevic where you discussed the army, and they would pay those -- that means, that the -- Serbia and Montenegro or what was left of Yugoslavia would take care of the salaries of -- of active-duty officers even if they would have then joined the VRS? Is that a correct understanding? Apart from whether they did it in full but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. That is correct. But could I just clarify it a bit? They were not willing to do that. Quite simply, there was a surplus of officers but we said, "We invested in that. Bosnia-Herzegovina has a right to this property of the JNA. We also allocated resources for the Yugoslav People's Army. We have the right at this point in time to participate in that." That is why, unwillingly, they accepted there and indeed they kept their promise that members of the army of Republika Srpska, active-duty officers, who used to be members of the Yugoslav People's Army, who voluntarily stayed in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the army of Republika Srpska, well, they would be paid by the Yugoslav People's Army or rather some kind of financial service of theirs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, can I just clarify one point? Mr. Bozidar Antic had been appointed minister of the economy, as we have it in English. Was he also Finance Minister or was there somebody else in that position?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. Mr. Antic was, as far as I can remember, Minister of the economy, whereas the Finance Minister was Momcilo Pejic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, straight away, I see that. It's in the minute of the meeting on the 22nd of April, he was the Deputy Prime Minister, wasn't he, with responsibility for finance, and it says, "and the economy"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes. I'm sorry, he was Deputy Prime Minister in charge of finance, but you're right, another person was Minister of Finance. I think it was Petra Markovic. But the Deputy Prime Minister, Mr. Pejic, was also in charge of that field of finance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's time for a break. We'll have a break until five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to go in private session for a second.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, could we then look now at the minute or record of the meeting of the 10th of May 1992 that's been in front of you for some time? The -- first of all, Mr. Krajisnik, do you remember whether you were at this meeting or not?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read this record, and I'm practically sure that I was not present at this session, but there was a consultative meeting with the government. Perhaps it was earlier on, but I don't think I attended this session, although I find all of this familiar. The agenda, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, when you refer to a consultative meeting with the government, consultative meeting between the government and whom?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this meeting, which is called a joint meeting of the council and the government, there was this meeting similar to this one between the negotiating team and the government, concerning the preparation of the assembly meeting. I know that that took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What would be the difference in practice, then, between a consultative meeting of the type you just mentioned and a meeting such as is recorded in this document that we are looking at?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There wouldn't be much of a difference, but here in this record there are certain decisions that I don't remember that we discussed at this consultative meeting. Somebody wrote this up later on. I mean, recorded what happened at that meeting where all of this was presented, all of this that is on this sheet of paper in front of me. So there wouldn't be much of a difference. I'm just saying that I do not remember this specifically. For example, these assignments that come later. I did not realise that that took place at the meeting that I attended. Mr. Kalinic and others. You have it here on page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then the -- it was decided, we see that there was to be an assembly session on the 12th of May, and an agenda proposed for the assembly session. You had been involved, had you, in the preparation of that agenda?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, I've already said. This should be after the meeting that I remember, that I'm the only one who remembers it at Jahorina. Well, they had a meeting and perhaps I attended it too, and then it was repeated what should be on the agenda. I did take part in establishing the agenda, and I even signed an invitation including the agenda, apart from one particular item, and then the MPs received this later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the first item, to make it clear, of course, this is the proposed agenda for the assembly session, and the first item, 1A, Report on the Political and War Situation. And that was to be made by the president of the national Security Council, and then Velibor Ostojic was charged with preparing the report with the assistance of, it was Mr. Stanisic, wasn't it, Minister of the Interior, and Mr. Subotic, minister for National Defence. Why was Mr. Ostojic the person charged with the preparation of that report?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic is a linguist by profession. He has a degree in Serbian, in the Serbo-Croat language, as it was called at the time. He was active in the party, that is to say that he cooperated closely with Mr. Karadzic, and he was on the government too. He was one of the very few ministers who was a member of the SDS. That is to say that it was this cooperation that led him by way of inertia to write this report on behalf of Mr. Karadzic. Now, how could he write a report? He could bring together the information that other government members had, the Minister of Defence, the Prime Minister, and I don't know who else, and then he would technically write up this report. Because he did not have all information, of course, he could not have written this autonomously. He technically wrote a report so that Mr. Karadzic would present it, although he did not read it later. Mr. Karadzic spoke off the cuff. He did not read the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then 6B, do you see the same document, just to clarify, it says 6B on the Obligations of Serbian Authorities Towards International Humanitarian Organisations, Dr. Kalinic in charge. Was that intended to mean Bosnian Serb authorities or wider?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This has to do with the Minister of Health and social affairs, Mr. Kalinic. We mentioned him already. He was in charge of cooperation with international humanitarian organisations, that primarily included the International Red Cross and the UNHCR and others too probably. So it is about the government of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and its minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then if we go, Mr. Krajisnik, to the second section, main section of this record or minute, do you see where it goes on to point 8? There is a heading in the middle, 2, and then it goes on to point 8, the state commission. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I want you to look at 9B, a decision to grant a subsidy from the budget to Pale municipality, "seeing that this municipality is overburdened by numerous refugees and has huge expenses related to the accommodation of relocated organs and the like." Was the -- was the refugee situation in Pale getting worse compared with how you described it earlier this week? I think it was earlier this week; I think it was yesterday. Earlier in your evidence anyway.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. I mean, it was slightly worse because at the very outset, it was extremely difficult, so it could have been, say, a bit worse. Suffice it to say that it was so hard at the very beginning and then there was this pressure of refugees coming from Sarajevo to Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik. I'd like you to put that document on one side, then, please, and be given the minutes and the record of the 16th session of the Assembly of the Serbian People.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's in P64A, tab 612, and the ERN is 00847711.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I've marked a lot of points in the margin, not because I'm necessarily going to ask you a question at every point where there is a letter. It's that much of the speeches are very long so it's not so easy and -- Your Honours, it's not so easy to find a point by saying, Well, so and so begins to speak because particular contributions go on for pages. I've basically just given us lots of markers there so, with a little bit of luck, we can find our way around pretty quickly. You have got a copy with letters and -- well, if you haven't got that, you can have one straight away, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think those letters are here. I haven't found a single one here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There is something that's just gone wrong, Mr. Krajisnik. There is one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart. Mr. Stewart, I think Mr. Krajisnik has been provided with a registry copy with no markings on it. Is that correct, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think that's what's happened, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps that should be returned to the Registrar and then he provide you, marked copy. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If it's 1A, then I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, it starts with A, and I'm afraid I ran out of letters in my own alphabet so towards the end we get some numbers as well. The -- now, we've heard about this meeting before, Mr. Krajisnik. I would like you to go straight to letter F in the margin which you will find at page 7, and it's at page 13 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this is Mr. Karadzic speaking and he has already been speaking at this point for quite a while, reporting on the war and the particular passage I'm looking at begins, "The Serbian side in Bosnia and Herzegovina." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "The Serbian side in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Presidency, the government, the Council for National Security which we have set up have formulated the strategic priorities, that is to say the strategic goals for the Serbian people." Now, Mr. Krajisnik, before we explore those goals which are hardly a mysterious item at this point in this case, how were the strategic goals formulated to go before this assembly meeting in Banja Luka? Who, when, and by what process were the strategic goals formulated?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I mentioned, we held a session at Jahorina, and we contacted Banja Luka and a certain number of deputies and were informed, or rather received two pieces of information. One was that they were unable to pass through and reach Pale, and secondly, we concluded that we had entered a stage in which a certain number of deputies would prefer not to attend the assembly but to continue acting as they had been. More than a month had gone by. Each one had his own autonomous region and had some sort of power. The general opinion was that the war was over, that we had done everything with the other side to reach a political solution and that there was simply nothing for us to discuss with them. This is very important. There was a feeling that we had been let down, that somebody did not want to respect the agreement we had reached, and which was incorporated into the principles that we should transform Bosnia and Herzegovina if we have given up the idea of Yugoslavia. As we had a certain number of deputies at Jahorina we decided to go to Banja Luka directly, all those deputies, and Mr. Mladic was there at the time because he was supposed to be appointed commander of the Main Staff. Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Koljevic were there but Mrs. Plavsic wasn't. The representatives of the government were there. And we considered how the negotiations could be continued especially in view of the fact that it had been announced that the negotiations had been suspended. After the last session the international community interrupted the negotiations. The idea was or rather people kept saying nobody knows what we are doing at these negotiations, nobody knows what the goals are, and I know. I participated in this. When we were preparing the session, we said, "Let us put what we said to Mr. Cutileiro down. Let's put it down into some kind of exposition so that those who listen will know what we are fighting for." When I use the word "fight," I'm referring to what happened at all the previous conferences. There was various disinformation. People were saying they have been betrayed this or that area. It's left out of the map. Nobody knows what they are doing because there hadn't been any sessions so that everything that is on the map, please, Your Honours, everything that was on our map, which we gave to Mr. Cutileiro, was included except for one additional goal, and that was the corridor. This was at the talks with the Croatian community in Graz. The problem was now something that was indispensable. The territory had to be a single territory. The Serb representatives did not want the Serb constituent unit to consist of several parts. There was a consultative meeting, not these minutes here, and we all got together and formulated these goals as briefly as possible, to avoid someone latching on to something and entering into a big discussion. We say separation, then we say the corridor, then we say part of Sarajevo, and so on. I can explain each one of these strategic goals and say what it was we wanted to present to these deputies. The goal was --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, just so that we go along the right track, perhaps I can make it clear that I am going to ask you questions which will give you the opportunity to explain each one of these strategic goals, so if you could wait for those questions we'll stay on the right track.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't going to explain but thank you. Thank you. It's you who are in charge of this, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Am in charge of my questions in the first place, Mr. Krajisnik, yes. What I was going to ask you next, Mr. Krajisnik, was this: The consultative meeting that you refer to, you say there was a consultative meeting, not these minutes here. You're talking about a consultative meeting in Pale, are you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Jahorina, where we -- I've just explained that -- memory of this. We saw there was no quorum so we had a meeting to discuss what to do, and that's when we agreed on this. There should be something in my view before this meeting. These items in these minutes -- well, the cabinet had a separate session. Maybe it was right after that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- who were present at the discussion before this assembly meeting when the strategic goals were put together in the way that you've described?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- I'm not asserting this -- I think that it was the usual people: Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Koljevic, Mr. Djeric, myself, the ministers. I'm not sure but I'm almost certain that it was those deputies who had arrived. They attended the meeting because it wasn't any special secret we were discussing but I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is there any possibility that Mr. Djeric was not involved in the formulation of the strategic goals?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe so. I think yes, but it's possible he was having a government session. I can't confirm this. I have to say that I know there was a group of people, I know, I participated in this. I know what the purpose was. But who exactly was there, all the people who were there, I can't be certain about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Had there been, before that consultative meeting, had there been discussion of a need or requirement to have some strategic goals, extending back over the previous few weeks?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. It was at that meeting, as one of the ways of preparing for the assembly, as we knew we would be asked what we were fighting for over there, what we were doing, that's when we had this idea and agreed on it. I don't know whether it was in the report. Mr. Karadzic put this forward but he did have a brief summary of the goals on a piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You said in a longish answer a few minutes ago, and Your Honours, this is at page 31, line 10, you said "the general opinion was that the war was over." First of all, is that what you said, as far as you recall?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said we contacted the deputies in Banja Luka and gained the impression that in many areas people thought that the negotiations were excluded and that there was no more war, that everybody had their own territory and they began to act as if all this was over. That's what I meant to say in connection with the telephone conversation with the representatives from Banja Luka, our deputies, and the impression. In the municipalities where one didn't feel the war, as one felt it around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, going back to the record of the Banja Luka assembly session, I want to ask you about the first goal, but to go back first on that point, do you find letter C in the margin, which should be at page 3 of your document, page 8 of the English?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm using that as a reference point, Mr. Krajisnik, because about -- well in the English it's about 30 lines, I don't know exactly what it would be in the Serbian, but there is a reference to Mr. Izetbegovic, so his name is probably in capital -- upper case letters. There is a passage that begins, "The Serbian people would not accept the unitarist Bosnia of Alija Izetbegovic." It's at the top of page 9, Your Honours, so easily, "and that is how we came to the conference on Bosnia and Herzegovina under European auspices." Can you find that passage, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see a reference to Alija Izetbegovic but I don't think that's it. Oh, yes, I found it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In World War II -- is that it? -- will not accept the unitarist Bosnia of Alija Izetbegovic. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's exactly it, Mr. Krajisnik. And then it continues: "At that conference, we have won a great political success, gaining the approval of the international community, in this case the European Community, for a three-part Bosnia and Herzegovina as opposed to the unitarist Bosnia and Herzegovina, a complex Bosnia and Herzegovina, consisting of three nation states, of three constitutive states whose relations and links will be stronger or weaker. We were for weaker, the Croats were for weaker, while in Europe they were for stronger links but that is less important. What is important is that in the political field we have won recognition of the legitimacy of our wish to have our own state unit in Bosnia and Herzegovina and that nobody has the right to dispute that. They may dispute a village or a municipality here and there, but nobody can dispute our right to have our own state unit, our own state organism or entity in Bosnia and Herzegovina." Mr. Krajisnik, in the way that that was presented there by Dr. Karadzic to the deputies, did that leave room for ambiguity in the minds of deputies as to whether Dr. Karadzic was talking about an independent, sovereign state of -- for the Serbs within Bosnia, recognised internationally as such, or whether he was talking about something which would fall within an internationally recognised state of Bosnia and Herzegovina containing all three parts?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have described the atmosphere. Mr. Karadzic stated clearly what we had achieved at the conference. We had achieved a tripartite solution. No one could speak of Bosnia-Herzegovina as an internationally recognised state because politically, at that point in time, this was very unpopular. But he did say clearly, "We have got our own constituent state." That was permissible to say. But within Bosnia and Herzegovina. There would be three constituent units and how they would be linked up, whether loosely or more firmly, well, that's another question. But there is no doubt about what Karadzic said. He tried to present this and interpret it in a way so as to win over the deputies who were angry and felt betrayed because Bosnia and Herzegovina had been recognised. This was his way of interpreting it, but it states quite clearly what we had achieved at the conference. Bosnia had been accepted and our constituent unit within it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krajisnik, it's correct, you and your co-negotiators, Mr. -- Dr. Karadzic and Professor Koljevic, you understood perfectly well, didn't you, that the European Community representatives and Mr. Cutileiro and others were not thinking in terms of a separate, internationally recognised state for Bosnian Serbs? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. From the very beginning, it was clear that Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina, Muslim Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatian Bosnia and Herzegovina in an alliance of Bosnian states cannot have anything more than internal autonomy and independence. The overarching umbrella so to speak would be an internationally recognised Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was beyond discussion. As for us, although later during the war, there were certain proposals by the international community but we'll come to those later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again the answer starts with absolutely not but from the explanation it appears that Mr. Krajisnik agrees with you that the aim was not separate, internationally recognised states but one state. Mr. Krajisnik is nodding yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour has absolutely anticipated the request for confirmation of the Trial Chamber's understanding that I was going to put forward. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, do you consider that that essential point was as clear to the deputies who attended the assembly session in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was clear to all of them, but their rhetoric, which came from some of the deputies, was inflamed by desires. If the Muslims had given up this compromise, they would have nothing further to do with them but it was clear to everybody what Dr. Karadzic was saying, at every session we provided information and we said that we had given up Yugoslavia, that we had accepted the compromise, and agreed to have Bosnia-Herzegovina become an internationally recognised entity.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Are you saying, Mr. Krajisnik, that it was clear to the deputies what it was that you, the negotiators, were saying about this, but that there was resistance among the deputies to accepting that position?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will be clear. From the moment when we changed our policy and let it be known that we could not respect the decision of the plebiscite and remain in Yugoslavia, there were constant complaints about why we had done this, and we had to explain hundreds of times why this had been done. This was a compromise. The desire to remain within Yugoslavia was something that people could not let go so easily and whenever an opportunity arose, it was expressed. In this case, they said that the agreement had been betrayed. We had said that, well, we have Bosnia and Herzegovina and our own constituent unit within it. Bosnia and Herzegovina will be internationally recognised. However, now the situation was that Bosnia and Herzegovina had been recognised but had not been transformed. And they said, Well, it's futile for you to negotiate with the other side because they will never respect this agreement. And now they were saying, Well, you see your attempts have been futile. Let's go another way. But after that, there would be just vagueness because nobody knew where they -- where to go next. That was what happened from the time we changed our policy and agreed to the compromise. War had broken up and the atmosphere was very heated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, was it -- well, I'll ask you this question first: Can you confirm, there was no difference between you and Dr. Karadzic at this point in relation to these strategic goals, was there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're always asking me between Mr. Karadzic and myself. Between Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Koljevic, Mr. Buha, and myself, most often there was no difference. So, yes, you're right. There was no difference between Mr. Karadzic and me. But this refers not just to the two of us but to all of us who participated in the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krajisnik, just explain the reason I ask you: It's Dr. Karadzic who was presenting these strategic goals at the assembly meeting. So you confirmed that. As far as the first goal is concerned, then, was it -- was it your intention, and you for these purposes can be at least the group that you've just mentioned, was it your intention that there should be any difference between this first goal and what you had hoped to achieve through the Cutileiro negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Stewart, Mr. Prosecutor, separation was the very foundation of the Cutileiro plan, its basis. And this meant drawing up internal demarcation lines among the three constituent units. Without that, there could be no three constituent units. One had to draw maps. It wasn't separation of peoples but separation of territories. This is written in an inept way, but to say Muslim Bosnia-Herzegovina will be over there, Croatian Bosnia and Herzegovina will be here, and Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina will be here, this was about setting up constituent units. There was no way to set them up but to separate the territories in this way. Separating the peoples, well, you can't do that without separating the territory. This is the fundamental transformation, drawing up three constituent units. I know that. Whoever says differently is wrong. I know that that's what we thought. Well, what about separating the people? It's not sending one people to the moon and the other people to Mercury. It meant drawing up demarcation lines within Bosnia. This wasn't done by someone else. I participated in it, and I know exactly what we did and what we thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours just on a practical matter because I'm not sure we put it on our list, at some point quite soon, I would like Mr. Krajisnik, not right this second, to have P47, which is that Official Gazette announcement of the six strategic objectives. Your Honour, we don't need it this second but if Mr. Registrar could very kindly fish that out, that will smooth things along.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, so let me put what is essentially the same question but I'm going to put it in a slightly different way: Was this first strategic goal intended to go any further than what had been proposed during the Cutileiro talks?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: With full liability, I assert that this was agreed from the beginning. As there is no Yugoslavia, we will have internal separation. Maps of the units will be drawn up. And this was never in dispute. Those units would be predominantly Serb, predominantly Muslim, predominantly Croatian, not exclusively Serb, Muslim or Croatian. Mr. Cutileiro proposed this, not to have certain territories cleansed or to create a Serbian state, but to have an area predominantly populated by Serbs where they would govern themselves. The Muslims were afraid to remain within Yugoslavia. They said that. But we had reason to be afraid of a unitary Bosnia because if they were outvoting us now, they would be doing the same later, unless we had our own constituent unit. If you don't want to be in Yugoslavia with us, then we want to have our own constituent unit here. It would have been borders, just like municipal borders or district borders. And I assert that that's how it was, under full liability. I have heard various interpretations but they are certainly not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krajisnik, returning to the record of the assembly session, page 13 of the English, it's page 7. It's where we were before, against letter F. We will be returning to that passage frequently because this is where Dr. Karadzic sets out the six strategic goals. So we will take them one by one. The second strategic goal, do you see that? It's the second paragraph after the letter F in the margin.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "The second strategic goal it seems to me is a corridor between Semberija and Krajina. That is something for which we may be forced to sacrifice something here and there but this is of the utmost strategic importance for the Serbian people because it integrates the Serbian lands not only of Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina but Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina with Serbia and the Serbian Krajina with Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbia. So that is a very important strategic goal which we have to achieve because there will be no Krajina, Bosnian Krajina, Serbian Krajina or alliance of Serbian states if we do not secure that corridor which will integrate us and give us an unimpeded flow from one part of our state to another." Now, first of all, Mr. Krajisnik, one thing is perfectly obvious, isn't it, it's in order to join up what you regarded as the Serb parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina itself, you had to have some such corridor. That's plain as can be, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And I can explain this rhetoric of Mr. Karadzic's, if you're interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, actually my question was going to betray interest in that topic, Mr. Krajisnik, so please do.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bosnian Krajina, that is to say Banja Luka, from April until the 12th of May, was completely sealed off. It even says in the newspapers that 12 babies died due to the lack of oxygen. And there was a lot of nervousness on the part of the MPs and the people of Bosnia and Bosnian Krajina, that they are sealed off and that they want to have communication with other parts because the other side, the Muslim side or the Croat side, would not let them go through. There were combinations when they took the highway and were escorted by UNPROFOR and so on and so forth. However, all that went down the drain. So there were these talks as to how to get them out of this ghetto. In order to resolve the situation, we talked about this corridor with the Croats. Again, on the basis of geographical principles of exchanging territories, in Graz. Now Mr. Karadzic is introducing a new objective. Your Honours, you will take the maps and you will see that there are some Serb villages in that blue, green, and yellow one. So territories should become more compact. But there is a part of territory that is missing, that's not Serb, in order to have this linked up. So then we thought that we would give the Croats some concessions near Kupres. Mr. Karadzic is saying here we will have to sacrifice some territories. That is on the political plane, territorially. Now, in that case, there would be this communication through the corridor. So the rhetoric was adapted to these people who we came to see, and who were so bitter because they were in a ghetto all the time. And what does that mean? They were encircled all the time. That is why this was presented here and I understand it fully, and perhaps others may not understand it if they cannot put all of this information together.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, when -- so had -- you say you had discussed this corridor with the Croats in Graz. Had there been any discussion with the Muslim side about such a corridor?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not then, but I can give you an example. Later on, there was even a map of this corridor and the solution that we had with the Croats. There is a map. But this was later. I can show you this map. By way of illustration, let me just say that Brcko was always a problem and they even suggested that it would go via Croatian territory. Then that we would have a bridge or a flyover so that the Muslims would go above and we would go underneath. There were different combinations, because there was a problem all the time with the Muslims, how to establish this corridor and how to handle things around Brcko. At that time we were not talking to Muslims because they didn't want to talk about any kind of transformation. They wanted the status question to remain. They had an independent state and they were no longer interested in negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In his description of the second strategic goal here, Dr. Karadzic obviously is including very clearly the notion of joining up the Serb parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He also refers to -- he says, it's in about the fourth or fifth line, he says, it's the third line of the English, "It is of the utmost strategic importance for the Serbian people because it integrates the Serbian lands not only of Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina but Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina with Serbia" and then a little later on, in the same paragraph, he says, "It's a very important strategic goal because without it," is what he's saying, "There will be no Krajina, Bosnian Krajina, Serbian Krajina, or alliance of Serbian states." What -- what was Dr. Karadzic -- as you understood it, what did he have in mind by referring to an alliance of Serbian states?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order for a project to be presented to the deputies, who keep thinking that they should return to Yugoslavia, to this common state, if I can put it that way, Mr. Karadzic spoke to them in stages. We have to resolve this in Bosnia and in the future, if the situation is right, let it be some kind of alliance of Serb states. Republika Srpska, Serb Krajina, Serbia, so on and so forth. So this is for political purposes so that this would be achieved now. And later you will see, Your Honours, gentlemen, what kind of debates took place in that parliament and you will see how much resistance there was to any kind of talks with those who had been betrayed us in terms of having Bosnia transformed and they were even angry at the European Community, which viewed this favourably. That is why this rhetoric was required. It was just this second objective that Mr. Karadzic was supposed to read out. But this was just the sugar coating so that they could accept this. And then later on we would appeal for negotiations. That was the objective. At any rate, I have to admit that if the international situation had been right then, for example for Serbs to say whether they wanted to live with Serbia or not or whether Serb Krajina would live with Serbia or not, everybody, well not exactly everybody, but a very large part would certainly say that they wanted to live with Serbs in Serbia rather than with Croats or Muslims from Bosnia because that is a natural right. But you are involved in real politics now, and you have Bosnia as it is and you have the international situation as it is. It is very hard to explain this wish to someone. On the one hand, you have people who are just talking without any obligations, and then you have to talk about what is doable. That is why this rhetoric was necessary in order to chart the course that was the only one possible. We were not the only ones in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You said in the course of that answer that it was just this second objective that Mr. Karadzic was supposed to read out. Are you saying that Mr. Karadzic went off script in some way at this point in the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. He just should read the first sentence, the other objective, because he had some written material in front of him but then perhaps he read this first sentence. As for the rest it was not in the material. He extemporised. He gave a free interpretation. He explained why it was necessary for them to understand why we were advocating the corridor. That was the point. And that is what I meant when I was speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was -- in the discussion and formulation of the strategic objectives before, and for the purposes of this assembly meeting, was there any specific discussion as to the width of this corridor?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
